metadata.title: Working and learning: A diversity of patterns (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The analysis uses OECD’s 2012 Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) microdata across 23 countries/regions, focusing on youth aged 16–29 and their work/study status. The excerpt does not report the specific complex-survey weight variables (e.g., student/sampling weights) or any replicate-weight scheme, so it is unclear whether population-representative weighted estimates were produced. The paper’s figures and pooled regressions are described as pooling across countries with country dummies, which is consistent with using the survey design but does not confirm the exact weighting implementation. For replication with PIAAC microdata, analysts should apply the official PIAAC student/sampling weights and replicate weights provided in the database to obtain correct standard errors under the complex sampling design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in the provided text are primarily incidence/probability outcomes (e.g., likelihood of work and study; multinomial categories) and descriptive/aggregate correlations, rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. While the paper references literacy proficiency scores, the excerpt does not specify whether these are PVs combined via Rubin’s rules or whether they are treated as scale scores/derived estimates. The missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case vs imputation) is not described in the excerpt, so the handling of missing questionnaire and proficiency inputs cannot be verified from the provided material.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper uses PIAAC 2012 and defines the baseline work-and-study population using the derived variable EDWORK: everyone aged 16–29 who reports being working and in education (EDWORK=2) is counted as a working student. Apprentices are treated as combining work and study irrespective of their EDWORK status: respondents identified as apprentices via C_q07 (current status including apprenticeship/internship) and/or D_q09 (contract type including apprenticeship/other training scheme) are added to the working-student total, and apprentices who are not reporting as working and/or not reporting as studying are handled to avoid inconsistencies. For VET programmes, the paper includes only VET students who declare they are working and studying (because VET status is defined via correspondence employed for VET status in highest educational qualification, and VET is only available at ISCED levels where academic vs vocational choice is possible, with some country exceptions). The excerpt does not specify additional exclusions (e.g., missing covariates) or whether analyses use complete cases.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD paper uses PIAAC 2012 to document how often youth aged 16–29 combine work and study across 23 countries/regions, and how this combination is structured by apprenticeship status, VET programmes, and other (non-formalised) arrangements. It reports that 39% of youth on average work while studying, with large cross-country variation (from under 20% in Italy/Czech Republic/Flanders to over 60% in the Netherlands). Using pooled probit and multinomial logit models with country dummies, it finds that older youth (20–29) are more likely to work and study, and that literacy proficiency is associated with a lower likelihood of combining study and work. It also shows that labour-market institutions and labour demand conditions—such as employment protection strictness, the difficulty of using temporary contracts, part-time incidence, and the minimum-to-median wage ratio—are related to the probability of work-and-study. The paper further reports that, after controlling for education and individual characteristics, youth combining work and study score about 5 literacy points higher than those studying only, but it emphasizes that PIAAC cannot establish individual-level causal effects or future labour-market outcomes.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD descriptive/associational analysis of work-and-study patterns using PIAAC, with regression-based marginal effects and multinomial logit models reported in the excerpt, but no machine-learning predictive modeling is described. Consequently, ML technique fields are empty and no ML target-variable findings can be tabulated under the ML schema. The excerpt also does not provide the final analytic sample size (N) or per-country student counts, so total_students and n_students remain null.
